A0102.title: Cross-Chain Bridge Smart Contract Auditing and Monitoring
A0102.definition: Conducting rigorous third-party audits of core cross-chain bridge contracts and implementing real-time monitoring mechanisms to detect anomalous transactions.
A0102.description: Vulnerabilities in cross-chain bridge smart contracts are a primary attack vector. Protective measures include: conducting security audits by multiple independent firms prior to deployment; performing formal verification of critical functions such as locking, minting, and burning; implementing on-chain monitoring systems to detect large transfers, abnormal minting, and unexpected contract calls; setting transaction limits and rate limiting, with additional verification or time delays required for single transfers exceeding thresholds; deploying emergency pause mechanisms to quickly freeze contracts upon detecting an attack; and conducting regular code reviews and bug bounty programs.
A0102.limitation: Audits cannot guarantee the discovery of all vulnerabilities, and novel attack techniques may bypass known detection methods; emergency pause mechanisms may be abused or become attack targets themselves; monitoring systems may generate false positives, impacting normal operations.
keywords: Cross-Chain Bridge Smart Contract Auditing and Monitoring

A0102-001.title: Layer2 Bridge Security Audit
A0102-001.description: Conduct professional third-party security audits and formal verification of cross-chain bridge/Layer2 bridge contracts, deploy multi-signature verification and delayed withdrawal mechanisms to prevent single-point private key compromise or contract vulnerabilities from being exploited to steal locked assets. The audit covers critical functions such as locking, minting, burning, and validator rotation, while multi-signature and timelocks provide an intervention window for anomalous operations.
A0102-001.definition: Professional audit of cross-chain bridge contracts, implementing multi-sig verification and delayed withdrawal mechanisms.
A0102-001.limitation: Audits can only cover known vulnerability patterns; novel attack vectors (e.g., flash loan combinatorial attacks, cross-protocol reentrancy) may still evade detection. If multi-signature private keys are centrally hosted or compromised via phishing/insider theft, the multi-signature mechanism becomes effectively useless. Attackers often use social engineering to control multi-signature holders or exploit the delayed withdrawal window to trigger panic-induced bank runs. Audit conclusions are time-sensitive; subsequent contract upgrades may introduce new vulnerabilities without re-audit, leading to protection failure.
